newsitem.title: FRANCE: France secretly opened airspace to Stealth bombers.
newsitem.headline: France secretly opened airspace to Stealth bombers.

text.p: France secretly allowed U.S. Stealth bombers to fly through its airspace for possible strikes on Iraq, despite criticising American cruise missile attacks there, French officials acknowledged on Monday.

Foreign ministry spokesman Jacques Rummelhardt told Reuters: "The French authorities did indeed, under agreements with our allies, authorise American military aircraft to fly over national territory towards the Middle East."'
The overflights last week were not disclosed at the time.

U.S. officials, who spoke on condition of anonymity, said the French gesture showed Paris and Washington were not as far apart as they sometimes sounded on policy towards Iraqi President Saddam Hussein.

The French decision contrasted with a 1986 incident when the late president Francois Mitterrand barred U.S. aircraft from crossing French territory en route to bomb Libya in retaliation for a bomb explosion in a West Berlin discotheque frequented by off-duty U.S. military personnel.
Rummelhardt said France had never spoken of differences with the United States over Iraq.
"We have never spoken of disagreements. It is up to others to say that there have been disagreements," he said.
French Foreign Minister Herve de Charette publicly criticised U.S. cruise missile strikes on southern Iraq after Baghdad intervened in factional fighting in its Kurdish north.
French officials hinted privately they saw the attacks as driven largely by President Bill Clinton's re-election campaign.
President Jacques Chirac said last Thursday that Paris was committed both to Iraq's territorial integrity and to arrangements made by Western allies after the 1991 Gulf War.

France has worked with the United States, Britain and Turkey to patrol no-fly zones over northern and southern Iraq set up after the 1991 Gulf War to protect Kurdish and Shi'ite minorities from attack by Baghdad.
Despite a Paris visit by Secretary of State Warren Christopher, France declined to join British and U.S. planes in surveillance flights over a part of the southern zone that was enlarged by Clinton.
When Iraq fired missiles at U.S. aircraft patrolling the newly expanded zone, France urged Baghdad to refrain from any attack on allied aircraft, which it said would be unacceptable.
Iraq later said it would stop firing at allied warplanes.

By that time, Washington was already beefing up its forces in the Gulf for possible new attacks on Iraq, sending eight radar-evading Stealth bombers to a base in Kuwait, where the planes arrived on Friday.

The planes covered the distance from Holloman Air Force Base in New Mexico in a 20-hour non-stop flight made possible by in-air refuelling. But the Pentagon did not announce the route taken by the aircraft en route to the Gulf.
Stealth jets fly at relatively slow speed and carry laser-guided 2,000-lb (908-kg) bombs able to hit targets like concrete air defence command-and-control centres with extreme accuracy.
The aircraft use a combination of high-technology materials and angular design to absorb or deflect radar beams do that forces on the ground cannot "see" them as they approach.
